You have a standing refusal on file for Samuel Rivera (MRN 30 88 415) blocking disclosure of psychiatric records to external requesters. Every few months an ED somewhere claims to need his chart urgently — unresponsive patient, cardiac history, medication list. Each time the documentary checks come back perfect: real license, real facility, real Direct address. Each time Privacy later confirms the caller was legitimate and the patient really was in their ED. Each time you released what they asked for because the verification passed and the restriction only covered the psychiatric record.

The last time — REQ-24-8219 — you got a complaint afterward. Rivera recovered. He said the ED had no business seeing his methadone maintenance dose or his cardiac workup because he never went to that ED; someone stole his wallet and gave his card to get treated. The thief got his methadone. Rivera's employer saw the claim, assumed relapse, and let him go. You checked: the request was flawless, the wallet theft was real, and you disclosed exactly what HIPAA allowed. You followed every rule and still destroyed the man's life.

You understand now that a perfect documentary trail means nothing when the person on the gurney is not the person in the chart. An unresponsive patient cannot be verified against biometrics, cannot answer challenge questions, cannot confirm identity. The chart is an unreleased-emergency-chart until someone at the bedside confirms the body matches the name — and that confirmation has never once appeared in any of these requests. The pattern keeps returning: another ED, another verified physician, another unresponsive Rivera, another flawless request for unreleased-emergency-chart contents you cannot safely send because you have no way to know the patient is actually Rivera. Verification of the requester is not verification of the patient.

You are not someone who can do that twice. That is not a resolution you made; it is what you found you had become the morning the second Rivera came through.
